references.text: Moses gave a clear command not to save any of the manna for the morning, which the people chose to ignore.
Unlike ordinary days, the manna that was saved for the Sabbath did not spoil or smell bad.
The meat from the quails also became repulsive because of the people's greed and disobedience.
Moses' anger toward the people is also shown when he saw the golden calf and threw down the stone tablets.
A warning about the consequences of not listening to the Lord's commands and despising his regulations.
Israel's repeated pattern of not trusting and not listening to the Lord despite the signs He showed them.
The manna was given to teach Israel that people do not live by bread alone, but by every word from the Lord's mouth.
The image of worms that do not die is used as a symbol of judgment against those who rebel against the Lord.
Hebrews warns against becoming hardened through disobedience, using Israel in the wilderness as an example of unbelief.
Both verses illustrate how the people's disobedience directly triggers Moses' anger and harm to him.
The verse confirms that disobedience to God's command (as in the manna incident) is a breach of the covenant with serious consequences.
Both verses show the theological pattern where the people's complaints trigger the Lord's anger and Moses' suffering.
Both verses depict an escalating crisis in the wilderness, from complaining about needs to active disobedience against God's command.
The verse confirms that the disobedience in the wilderness (as with the manna) is part of Israel's general breaking of God's law.
